## What You Will Build

A short Quarto page and a Reveal.js deck, built with a coding agent.
The supplied wine data gives us a concrete example.

| During the three hours | After the workshop, if useful |
|---|---|
| `hello.qmd` → reviewed `hello.html` | Six-slide wine introduction |
| Deliberate error → diagnosis → repaired render | Three-page wine essay and runnable notebook |
| `talk.qmd` → Reveal.js slides → optional Quarto Pub URL | Separate wine-chemistry blog |

::: {.notes}
Learning objectives: request an implementation, read Markdown/YAML/code,
check rendered results, diagnose a deliberate failure, change an output
format, and review publication. Audience: students new to Quarto, with basic
folder and terminal familiarity. Three-hour completion means an inspected
HTML page, a repaired render, and a reviewed Reveal.js deck. The dataset is
classification data, not wine quality or tasting data. Source: UCI Wine dataset,
checked 2026-10-21.
:::

## The Wine Question {#wine-question}

Imagine three unlabeled groups of wine bottles. A lab measures each sample's
chemistry. Could those measurements help identify its cultivar?

| What we have | What we do not have |
|---|---|
| 178 samples, three anonymous cultivar labels | Named grapes or tasting scores |
| 13 measured features per wine | A guarantee about new regions or vintages |

We will begin with **alcohol** and **color intensity**, then inspect how
individual wines overlap even when group averages differ.

::: {.notes}
UCI describes samples from one Italian region and three cultivars. Cultivar
numbers 1–3 are categories, not ranks. Color intensity has no unit specified
on the UCI page. The local CSV is a scikit-learn copy with added sample IDs.
UCI and scikit-learn documentation checked 2026-10-21.
:::

## Can Two Measurements Separate the Cultivars? {#wine-preview}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-wine-preview
#| fig-cap: "Alcohol versus color intensity for 178 UCI wine samples. Colors show anonymous cultivar labels."
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of alcohol and color intensity for 178 wines in three cultivar groups. The groups differ but overlap, especially around the center of the plot."
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

wine = pd.read_csv("examples/wine-context/wine.csv")
with plt.style.context("dark_background"):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
    for label, group in wine.groupby("cultivar"):
        ax.scatter(group.alcohol, group.color_intensity, label=f"Cultivar {label}",
                   s=34, alpha=0.8)
    ax.set_xlabel("Alcohol (dataset measurement)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Color intensity (dataset measurement)")
    ax.legend(title="Anonymous label", ncol=3, loc="upper center")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

**Look closely:** where do the colors overlap? This plot describes the supplied
wines; it is not a test of classification accuracy.

::: {.notes}
The caption and labels describe a real, local dataset, not invented teaching
counts. One point is one wine sample. Both axes show the dataset's recorded
values; UCI does not give physical units for these columns. Ask learners to
locate overlap before they see group means.
:::

## Three-Hour Workshop Route

| Time | Focus | Checkpoint |
|---|---|---|
| 00:00–01:00 | Anatomy & the agent | Rendered `hello.html` and a precise revision |
| 01:00–01:10 | Break | |
| 01:10–02:00 | Execution & formatting | CLI diagnosis and repaired output |
| 02:00–02:10 | Break | |
| 02:10–03:00 | Outputs & publishing | Reviewed `talk.html`; optional Quarto Pub URL |

: {tbl-colwidths="[19,41,40]"}

**Working pattern:** ask the agent → inspect its edits → render → inspect the
output → revise. The four wine projects later in the deck extend this path.

::: {.notes}
Audience: students new to Quarto. Prerequisites: opening a folder,
using an editor, and basic terminal navigation. No environment-manager expertise
is assumed. Allow roughly 15 minutes for orientation, 45 minutes for Hour 1,
50 minutes for Hour 2, and 50 minutes for Hour 3. Teach prompts live and
inspect the actual files and browser. Publishing is optional.
:::

## How to Use These Slides

Most slides repeat one three-part pattern:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Ask your coding agent**

Paste the plain-English request into your agent session.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Commands**

See what performs the work, or run the step yourself.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Check**

Inspect an observable result before continuing.
:::
::::

The agent can edit files and run local tools, subject to its permissions.
You do not need to repeat a command it has already completed.

## Before You Begin

- Install [Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/), Git, and an editor.
- Install one coding agent using the next three slides, then open your working folder.
- Sign in with an account that can use your chosen tool.
- Have a GitHub account and [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com/) for publishing.

The terminal examples use macOS, Linux, or WSL on Windows.
The same prompts work with Claude Code, Codex, or Antigravity CLI.

## Install Claude Code {#install-claude}

On macOS, Linux, or WSL, run once in your terminal:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
```

Open a new terminal, then check and start it:

```bash
claude --version
claude
```

Complete sign-in with an account that has Claude Code access.
Choose one coding agent for the exercises.

[Official setup and other platforms](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup).
Verified **2026-10-06**.

::: {.notes}
Run the installer yourself before the workshop. These fences are display-only.
Start the agent inside the exercise folder once it is created. Do not run two
agents as simultaneous writers in the same directory.
:::

## Install Codex {#install-codex}

With Node.js and npm available, run once in your terminal:

```bash
npm install -g @openai/codex@latest
codex --version
codex
```

Complete the sign-in flow with an account authorized to use Codex.
Start it inside your exercise folder, or select that folder in a graphical client.

[Official CLI guide](https://developers.openai.com/codex/cli/) and
[npm installation example](https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/codex/using_goals_in_codex).
Verified **2026-10-06**.

::: {.notes}
Install only the tool you plan to use. Record its version. Installation and
sign-in are preparation; later prompts use the term coding agent for any of them.
:::

## Install Google's Terminal Agent {#install-antigravity}

For an individual Google account, install **Antigravity CLI** on macOS or Linux:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://antigravity.google/cli/install.sh | bash
```

Open a new terminal, then check and start it:

```bash
agy --version
agy
```

Complete the interactive setup and sign in with an eligible Google account.
Choose one coding agent for the exercises.

[Official installation guide](https://antigravity.google/docs/getting-started?tab=cli).
Verified **2026-10-28**.

::: {.notes}
Google moved individual free, Pro, and Ultra Gemini CLI access to Antigravity
CLI in June 2026. Gemini CLI remains supported for certain enterprise licenses
and paid API key access. Use the official guide for Windows installation.
The installer command is display-only; never execute it while rendering.
Google's [transition announcement](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/discussions/28017)
and installation guide were checked 2026-10-28.
:::

# Hour 1 · Anatomy & the Agent

## A Folder for the Workshop

**Terminal, once:** choose a new folder outside this workshop repository.

```bash
mkdir -p ~/code/quarto-play
cd ~/code/quarto-play
# Start one coding agent:
claude
# Or: codex
# Or: agy
```

**Ask your coding agent:**

> I am learning Quarto. Use this folder for the exercises. Check the tools
> available, initialize Git if needed, and work on a workshop branch.
> Tell me which folder you are using and what is missing.

**Check:** the session names `quarto-play` as its working folder.

::: {.notes}
In a graphical coding agent client, select the same local folder and enter the prompt
in the conversation. The CLI route makes the working directory explicit without
depending on a particular app layout. Git equivalents: git init --initial-branch=main
and git switch -c workshop. Initial branches can be unborn until the first commit.
:::

## Connect Your GitHub Account {#connect-github}

**Ask your coding agent in `quarto-play`:**

> Check whether GitHub CLI (`gh`) is available here. If it is missing, help me
> install it for this terminal. Guide me through signing in to my GitHub account
> in the browser, then verify the active account. Do not create a repository yet.

**Commands to recognize:**

```bash
gh auth login
gh auth status
```

**Check:** `gh auth status` names the GitHub account you intend to use.

[GitHub CLI login](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_auth_login) and
[status](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_auth_status), checked 2026-10-28.

::: {.notes}
If learners use WSL, run `gh` in that same WSL terminal. The browser sign-in
may open outside WSL; learners complete the device-code flow themselves.
Do not paste tokens into the coding-agent conversation. This step connects
GitHub before publication without creating or pushing a remote repository.
:::

## A Document from One Request {#first-request}

**Ask your coding agent:**

> Create hello.qmd, a short HTML page for a student new to Quarto. Set
> `format: html` in its YAML frontmatter. Include a
> title, a brief explanation, and two things I can publish. Show Markdown for
> a heading, bold phrase, and list beside its rendered result. Add a
> self-contained Mermaid diagram of a .qmd file becoming HTML. Render, fix
> errors, and tell me which file to open.

**Command behind the render:**

```bash
quarto render hello.qmd --to html
```

**Check:** compare `hello.qmd` with `hello.html`. The Markdown example matches
its rendered result, and the diagram is visible.

::: {.notes}
Live demonstration: send the request, show file edits and the actual render
command, then open the output. Do not substitute the agent's completion message
for the rendered page. If dependencies are missing, use the setup prompt below.
:::

## What the Coding Agent Did

| Your request | Work to inspect |
|---|---|
| “Create hello.qmd” | A new editable source file |
| “A short HTML page” | YAML selecting HTML and concise Markdown |
| “Show a Markdown example” | Source syntax and its rendered result |
| “Add a simple graphic” | A visible graphic defined in the source |
| “Render it” | A Quarto command and its output |
| “Fix any build errors” | Further edits and a successful rerun |

The coding agent can carry out this sequence from a plain-English request.
The generated source remains yours to read, edit, and version.

> Change the title to “Can Chemistry Distinguish Wine Cultivars?”. Add a

> Add sections for code, interpretation, and sources. Render again.

**Check:** both titles change. This HTML practice page can later support the

## Understanding the Source

## Quarto's Job

Quarto combines prose, code, and results into a publication.
The coding agent can write the source and run Quarto for you.

| Source | Role |
|---|---|
| Markdown | Headings, paragraphs, links, lists |
| YAML | Title, output format, document options |
| Executable cells | Computation and generated figures |
| CSS | Appearance of HTML pages and slides |

### Exercise

Browse the [Quarto gallery](https://quarto.org/docs/gallery/). Describe one
feature you would ask your coding agent to add to your project.

## The Quarto Rendering Pipeline {#render-pipeline}

```text
hello.qmd
   │  executable chunks, if present
   ▼
Jupyter (often Python) or Knitr (often R)
   │  code and results become Markdown
   ▼
intermediate .md
   │  document conversion
   ▼
Pandoc
   ├── HTML page or Reveal.js slides
   └── PDF (with a PDF engine)
```

**When a render fails:** locate the source/YAML, code-execution, or output
conversion stage before asking the agent for a fix.

::: {.notes}
The execution stage is skipped when there are no executable chunks. Quarto can
also run filters and format-specific tools around Pandoc; this is a teaching
model. The intermediate Markdown can be temporary. Source: Quarto's rendering
overview, https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/hello/positron.html
(checked 2026-10-28).
:::

## One Plain-Text Source, Many Outputs {#quarto-flow}

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-width: 12
flowchart LR
    A["Plain-text Markdown<br/>hello.qmd"] --> B["Quarto"]
    B --> C["HTML page"]
    B --> D["PDF document"]
    B --> E["Word document"]
    B --> F["Reveal.js slides"]
```

The `.qmd` file stays editable. Quarto renders the requested format; some
formats need additional tools or document settings.

::: {.notes}
This graphic shows representative outputs, not a claim that every source
renders unchanged to every format. Markdown supplies the prose and structure;
YAML, code cells, and other Quarto features can extend the same source.
Ask learners which file they would edit to change wording in every output.
:::

## Markdown You Can Recognize

**Ask your coding agent:**

> Add a “Reading list” to hello.qmd with a link to the UCI Wine dataset
> and one bold phrase explaining that cultivar labels are anonymous.
> Verify the link, render, and explain the Markdown.

**Source pattern:**

```{.markdown code-line-numbers="1|3|5"}
## Reading list

The **cultivar labels are anonymous categories**.

[UCI Wine dataset](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/109/wine)
```

**Check:** a heading, bold text, and a working link appear on the page.

## YAML Selects the Output

**Ask your coding agent:**

> Add a table of contents to hello.qmd. Keep the existing title and
> sections. Render it and explain the YAML change.

**Source pattern at the top of the file:**

```yaml
---
title: "Can Chemistry Distinguish Wine Cultivars?"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
---
```

**Check:** the contents links lead to your section headings.

## Prompt Engineering for Quarto {#prompt-vocabulary}

Name the part to change, the action, and the visible check.

| Precise term | What it identifies |
|---|---|
| **YAML frontmatter** | Metadata between the opening `---` lines |
| **format option** | `html`, `pdf`, or `revealjs` output |
| **Markdown heading** | A section or slide title in the body |
| **code chunk** | Executable code in a `{python}` or `{r}` fence |
| **chunk execution options** | `#|` controls such as `echo` and `fig-cap` |

**Try:** “Change the YAML `format` to `html`; add a caption to the plot chunk;
render and check that the caption appears.”

::: {.notes}
Ask learners to point to one of these parts in `hello.qmd`. Precise vocabulary
helps the agent edit the intended part and helps the learner review the diff.
Official references: https://quarto.org/docs/computations/execution-options.html
and https://quarto.org/docs/presentations/revealjs/ (checked 2026-10-28).
:::

## Formatting a Comparison

**Ask your coding agent:**

> Add two tabs to hello.qmd: “Question” and “Evidence”. Put a
> short wine-data note in each. Use Quarto's tabset syntax and render.

**Source pattern:**

```markdown
::: {.panel-tabset}
## Question
Can chemistry distinguish the three cultivars?
## Evidence
Alcohol and color intensity vary, with some overlap.
:::
```

**Check:** clicking each tab reveals the corresponding text.

# Hour 2 · Execution & Formatting

## Displayed Code and Executed Code

**Ask your coding agent:**

> Add one displayed Python example and one executable Python cell to
> hello.qmd. Have each say hello. Explain how their fences differ.
> Render the page with execution enabled.

````markdown
```python
print("This code is displayed")
```

```{{python}}
print("This code runs")
```
````

**Check:** only the executable cell produces a separate output line.

## The Coding Agent Handles the Runtime

If the executable example needs dependencies, **ask your coding agent:**

> Inspect the available Python environments. Reuse a suitable local
> environment or prepare one for this project. Render hello.qmd with
> execution enabled. Fix failures and record the interpreter, dependencies,
> and working command in README.md.

**Commands you should recognize:**

```bash
quarto check jupyter
quarto render hello.qmd
```

**Check:** the output exists and the recorded build command works.

::: {.notes}
The selected interpreter may require an environment variable or activation.
Have the agent record the actual invocation, rather than teaching a universal
environment fix. Optional reproducibility recipes are in the workshop repository.
:::

## A Computation in These Slides

This cell counts the three cultivar groups from the supplied CSV when the
deck renders:

```{python}
#| echo: true
import csv
from collections import Counter

with open("examples/wine-context/wine.csv", newline="") as source:
    group_counts = Counter(row["cultivar"] for row in csv.DictReader(source))
total = sum(group_counts.values())
largest_share = 100 * max(group_counts.values()) / total
print(f"Wine samples: {total}")
print(f"Largest group share: {largest_share:.1f}%")
```

**Check:** the total is 178. The largest group contains 71 wines.

## Revise a Calculation

The `max` function selects the largest cultivar group. What happens if we
ask for the smallest group instead?

### Exercise

> Add this computation to hello.qmd, adjusting the CSV path to
> `context/wine.csv`. Change `max` to `min`, render, and explain what changes.

**Check:** the total stays 178 while the reported group share changes.

## Cell Options Control What Readers See

**Ask your coding agent:**

> Hide the group-count calculation's code in the page, but keep its output
> visible and recompute it on render. Explain the option used.

**Source pattern inside the executable cell:**

```python
#| echo: false
import csv
from collections import Counter
with open("context/wine.csv", newline="") as source:
    group_counts = Counter(row["cultivar"] for row in csv.DictReader(source))
print(f"Wine samples: {sum(group_counts.values())}")
```

`echo: false` hides source. `eval: false` would stop the calculation.

**Check:** the result remains visible and agrees with the practice inputs.

## Controlled Failure {#controlled-failure}

### Exercise

Copy this **deliberately broken** chunk into your practice `hello.qmd`.
Ask the agent to render **without fixing the chunk first**:

````markdown
```{{python}}
# Deliberate error: this name has not been defined.
print(workshop_total_typo)
```
````

Then ask: “Quote the first useful error in the Quarto CLI output. Point to
the failing chunk, explain the cause, and propose the smallest fix. Do not
change unrelated text.” Apply the fix, render again, and inspect the output.

::: {.notes}
Give about 15 minutes. The broken chunk is display-only in this deck; learners
copy it into their own `hello.qmd`. Have them run `quarto render hello.qmd` or
ask the agent to run it. Scan the CLI output from the bottom for
`NameError: name 'workshop_total_typo' is not defined`, then move upward to the
cell and line. Distinguish this Python exception from the surrounding
Jupyter/Quarto stack frames. Ask which file and chunk failed before accepting
the agent's explanation. A minimal repair is to define the intended value
before printing it or replace the mistaken name with the correct variable.
If the agent invents a package problem, ask it to quote the CLI evidence.
Rerender and compare source and output. Exact stack frames vary by version.
:::

## Check the Diagnosis

| CLI evidence | Request to the agent |
|---|---|
| YAML parse error before execution | “Show the frontmatter line and valid indentation.” |
| Python `NameError` in a chunk | “Trace this name to its definition.” |
| Pandoc or PDF engine error | “Identify the output stage and missing tool.” |

Require the agent to quote the relevant error and show the smallest source
change. A successful rerender tests the explanation.

::: {.notes}
The controlled failure uses the middle row. The other rows connect this
exercise to the rendering pipeline; they are not additional required failures.
:::

# Hour 3 · Outputs & Publishing

## Change HTML to Reveal.js {#html-to-revealjs}

Ask the agent to copy the repaired `hello.qmd` to `talk.qmd` and change its
YAML format from `html` to `revealjs`:

````yaml
---
title: "My short talk"
format: revealjs
---
````

Use `##` headings for individual slides. Ask the agent to split long sections
and keep each result with its meaning. Then render:

```bash
quarto render talk.qmd
```

**Check:** open `talk.html` and advance through every slide.

::: {.notes}
The learner's `hello.qmd` may use the nested `format: html: toc: true` form
shown earlier. In that case, ask the agent to replace that entire `format`
block with `format: revealjs`; do not leave an `html`-only option under it.
Use the copy to compare HTML and slide outputs. Quarto's Reveal.js guide
confirms the format value and level-two slide headings:
https://quarto.org/docs/presentations/revealjs/ (checked 2026-10-28).
:::

## Review the Slides Before Sharing

**Ask your coding agent:**

> Render `talk.qmd`, inspect every slide at desktop and laptop presentation
> sizes, and report text overflow or missing results. Fix the source and
> rerender. Tell me which slides changed.

**Check yourself:** Can someone read every slide? Do links work? Is a computed
result still explained? Is any private note or local path visible by mistake?

::: {.notes}
Use roughly 1440 × 1000 for desktop and 1366 × 768 for laptop. The learner
signs off on the deck. Allow about 15 minutes for review and revision.
:::

## Publish the Reviewed Deck to Quarto Pub {#publish-quarto-pub}

In your **practice folder**, after checking the destination and output:

```bash
quarto publish quarto-pub talk.qmd
```

Follow Quarto's interactive account and destination prompts. Open the returned
URL and confirm the public deck matches your reviewed local `talk.html`.

**Agent request:** “Prepare the publish command and tell me what it will make
public. Wait for my approval before running it.”

::: {.notes}
Demonstrate with an instructor-owned example or let participants publish
their own. Do not publish this workshop repository: its `docs/` directory is
served from main by GitHub Pages. Quarto documents the command and interactive
setup at https://quarto.org/docs/cli/publish.html and
https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/quarto-pub.html (checked 2026-10-28).
Quarto Pub content is public. Allow about 15 minutes, including URL check.
:::

## Three-Hour Completion Check

### Exercise

Show a partner `hello.qmd`, the rendered HTML, the repaired error, and
`talk.html`. If you published, show the Quarto Pub URL too. Explain:

1. Where YAML frontmatter, Markdown, and code each live.
2. Which CLI line identified the deliberate failure.
3. What changed when `html` became `revealjs`.
4. What you reviewed before sharing.

**Done:** your partner can reproduce the render and follow your diagnosis.

::: {.notes}
Allow the final 10 minutes for this check and questions. Publishing is
optional; a reviewed local deck and the exact publish command demonstrate the
workflow without requiring a public account. The next slides are follow-on
wine-data projects, not required in the three-hour core.
:::

# Follow-on Wine Projects

## Four Optional Deliverables

The same agent workflow can produce a six-slide wine introduction, a
three-page essay, a runnable notebook, and a separate blog. Use the supplied
UCI Wine data and inspect each output before sharing it.

These projects extend the workshop; they are not required in three hours.

# Task 1: Wine Chemistry Introduction Slides

## Shared Inputs for Tasks 1–3 {#wine-inputs}

From the workshop clone, copy the teaching bundle into your practice folder:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/code/quarto-play/context
cp examples/wine-context/* ~/code/quarto-play/context/
```

| Input | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `wine.csv` | 178 real wine samples and 13 measured features |
| `notes.md` | Provenance, definitions, limits, and task checks |
| `sources.bib` | UCI and scikit-learn source records |
| `notebook.qmd` | Worked data notebook source |

**Check:** return to your `quarto-play` agent session. Preserve the CSV.

## Task 1: A Generated Introduction {#task-slides}

**Ask your coding agent in `quarto-play`:**

> Create intro.qmd for first-year data science students. Generate exactly
> six Reveal.js slides: title, the mystery-cultivar question, what one row
> and the labels mean, two chemical features, overlap and limits, and sources.
> Use context/notes.md and context/sources.bib. Keep the dark theme, add
> speaker notes, and render intro.html.

```bash
quarto render intro.qmd --to revealjs
```

**Outputs:** `intro.qmd` and `intro.html`, six slides including title and sources.

**Check:** explain the question without claiming these are wine-quality scores.
Inspect every slide at desktop and laptop sizes, including links and captions.

# Task 2: A Three-Page Essay

## Task 2: What Can Chemistry Tell Us? {#task-essay}

**Ask your coding agent in `quarto-play`:**

> Write essay.qmd for data science students about what the UCI wine
> measurements can tell us about three anonymous cultivars. Use
> context/wine.csv for all numbers and context/sources.bib for provenance.
> Explain group counts, means, variation, and overlap; distinguish
> description from prediction. Follow the page plan on the next slide.
> Render exactly three pages to essay.pdf and inspect them.

```bash
quarto render essay.qmd --to pdf
```

**Outputs:** editable `essay.qmd` and a three-page `essay.pdf`.

## Essay Page Plan and Review

| Page | Argument |
|---|---|
| 1 | Question, dataset provenance, unit of analysis, cultivar labels |
| 2 | Alcohol and color intensity: counts, means, spread, overlap |
| 3 | What the descriptive evidence cannot establish; references |

Use A4 paper, 11-point text, and 1-inch margins. **Three pages total**,
including references, with no separate cover. Revise prose to fit.

### Exercise

Trace each numerical claim to `context/wine.csv`. Find one sentence that
overstates the evidence and ask your agent to revise it.

::: {.notes}
Ask the agent to inspect the available PDF engine and record the build command.
Keep the prose in essay form. Group statistics describe these 178 wines, not
all wine. Color intensity has no unit specified in the source; avoid inventing
one. PDF guidance checked 2026-10-19:
https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/pdf-basics.html.
:::

# Task 3: A Data Jupyter Notebook

## Task 3: Notebook Content {#task-notebook}

**Ask your coding agent in `quarto-play`:**

> Adapt context/notebook.qmd into notebook.qmd here. Fix data and
> bibliography paths to context/. Include the question, sample counts,
> group means, medians, sample standard deviations, and a captioned
> alcohol-versus-color scatterplot. State what a row represents and what
> the labels mean. Include limitations and readable source links in
> Markdown. Convert to notebook.ipynb and execute it with saved results.

**Outputs:** editable `notebook.qmd` and runnable `notebook.ipynb`.

**Check:** all 178 rows contribute; summaries and plot agree with the CSV.

## Task 3: A Runnable Jupyter Notebook

Run in `quarto-play` with the selected Python/Jupyter environment:

```bash
quarto convert notebook.qmd --output notebook.ipynb
jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute --inplace notebook.ipynb
```

### Exercise

Open `notebook.ipynb`, restart its kernel, and run all cells from the task folder.

**Done:** code cells execute, saved table and chart agree with the CSV,
and source links work. An HTML page alone does not complete this task.

::: {.notes}
Quarto conversion preserves executable cells. In validated Quarto 1.6.40,
rendering directly to IPYNB can turn analysis code into Markdown. Official
conversion and nbconvert guidance checked 2026-10-19:
https://quarto.org/docs/cli/convert.html and
https://nbconvert.readthedocs.io/en/latest/usage.html.
:::

# Task 4: A Separate Blog

## A Separate Blog Folder

**Terminal, once:** start a separate blog project and coding agent session.

```bash
mkdir -p ~/code/quarto-blog
cd ~/code/quarto-blog
# Start one coding agent:
claude
# Or: codex
```

**Ask your coding agent:**

> Create a Quarto blog titled “Wine Chemistry Notebook”.
> Initialize Git if needed and work on a blog-setup branch. Render the
> starter site and tell me how to preview it locally.

**Output:** an HTML website with a home page and a wine-chemistry post.
**Check:** the home page lists the starter posts before you add your own.

## The Scaffold Command

The coding agent can run the scaffold command as part of that request:

```bash
quarto create project blog . --no-open --no-prompt
```

| Generated path | What to inspect |
|---|---|
| `_quarto.yml` | Site title, navigation, theme |
| `index.qmd` | Post listing |
| `posts/` | A folder for each post |
| `posts/_metadata.yml` | Shared post defaults |
| `about.qmd` | About page |

**Check:** the coding agent edits the generated configuration without losing its structure.

::: {.notes}
The flags skip editor launch and confirmation. Run this command only in the
new blog folder, and only if your coding agent has not already scaffolded it.
Source: https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-blog.html (checked 2026-10-06).
:::

## Choose What the Blog Publishes {#blog-render-targets}

**Ask your coding agent:**

> In the blog's _quarto.yml, restrict project.render to the home page,
> about page, and posts. Keep context/ as source material for the analysis.
> Preserve the existing site configuration.

```yaml
project:
  type: website
  render:
    - index.qmd
    - about.qmd
    - posts/**/*.qmd
```

**Check:** after rendering, `_site/context/notes.html` and
`_site/context/notebook.html` are absent. Add any new public pages to the list.

::: {.notes}
By default, Quarto renders Markdown and notebook inputs throughout a project.
The copied context bundle includes notes.md and notebook.qmd, so a default blog
would turn both into extra public pages. An explicit render list keeps these
inputs available to the post without rendering them as pages. This controls
render targets, not access to files explicitly copied as website resources.
Official render-target documentation checked 2026-10-19:
https://quarto.org/docs/projects/quarto-projects.html#render-targets.
:::

## Wine Context for the Post {#wine-context}

Copy the shared teaching inputs into the separate blog:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/code/quarto-blog/context
cp ~/code/quarto-play/context/* ~/code/quarto-blog/context/
```

| Input | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `wine.csv` | 178 samples and three anonymous cultivars |
| `notes.md` | Question, provenance, and limits |
| `sources.bib` | UCI and scikit-learn references |
| `notebook.qmd` | Worked data notebook to adapt |

**Check:** cultivar numbers are categories, not quality ratings.

::: {.notes}
Run the copy commands in a terminal, then return to the blog agent session.
The preceding slide excludes this bundle from the blog's render list.
:::

## Your First Executable Post

**Ask your coding agent:**

> Read context/notes.md and context/notebook.qmd. Create
> posts/wine-chemistry/index.qmd with a question, executable Python reading
> wine.csv, an alcohol-versus-color scatterplot, interpretation, and cited
> sources. Fix paths for the post folder. Include title, date, caption, and
> alt text. Render the blog and check its listing.

```bash
quarto render
```

**Outputs:** `posts/wine-chemistry/index.qmd`,
`_site/posts/wine-chemistry/index.html`, and a listing in `_site/index.html`.

**Check:** the chart shows three labeled groups and the home page links to the post.

## A Cell the Coding Agent Might Write

One possible source pattern inside `posts/wine-chemistry/index.qmd`:

````markdown
```{{python}}
#| label: fig-wine
#| fig-cap: "Alcohol and color intensity in 178 UCI wine samples."
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot colored by three anonymous cultivars, with overlap."
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
wine = pd.read_csv("../../context/wine.csv")
for label, group in wine.groupby("cultivar"):
    plt.scatter(group.alcohol, group.color_intensity,
                label=f"Cultivar {label}", alpha=0.7)
plt.xlabel("Alcohol (dataset measurement)")
plt.ylabel("Color intensity (dataset measurement)")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
```
````

**Check:** each point represents one sample; the labels remain anonymous.

## Provenance and Limits {#wine-notes}

**Ask your coding agent:**

> Cite the UCI Wine dataset for the measurements and scikit-learn for
> the local export. Explain the row and cultivar labels. State that this
> chart describes the supplied wines; it does not measure prediction
> accuracy or wine quality. Render the references.

- [UCI Wine dataset](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/109/wine)
- [scikit-learn `load_wine`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.datasets.load_wine.html)

**Check:** the post has working source links and a specific limitation.

::: {.notes}
UCI and scikit-learn documentation checked 2026-10-21. The labels identify
three cultivars but supply no named grapes, tasting scores, or sampling design.
:::

## Preview and Render

**Ask your coding agent:**

> Start a local preview of this blog and give me its URL. I want to
> inspect the post, the listing, and the navigation in a browser.

**Commands for your own terminal:**

```bash
quarto preview
# When you need a fresh output build:
quarto render
```

Preview serves the site while you edit. Render creates the output files.
Neither command publishes the blog to the public web.

## Four Task Completion Checks {#task-checklist}

- **Introduction slides:** `intro.html` has exactly six readable slides,
  including the title and references.
- **Essay:** `essay.pdf` has exactly three pages including references
  and explains what the descriptive summaries can support.
- **Data Jupyter notebook:** `notebook.ipynb` runs from a fresh kernel
  and saves the group summaries and chart for all 178 wines.
- **Separate blog:** the HTML home page links to the rendered wine-chemistry post.

For every task, keep editable sources, unchanged inputs, and a `README.md`
with build commands. Check source links, provenance, and the unit of analysis.

# Review and Publication

## Reviewing the Files

**Ask your coding agent:**

> Summarize the changes and explain which files are source, generated
> output, or local dependencies. Check the diff and suggest the files
> that belong in a commit. Keep this review local.

**Commands for inspection:**

```bash
git status --short
git diff --stat
git diff --check
```

**Check:** inspect new files too. A normal `git diff` omits untracked files.

## Publishing Preparation

**Ask your coding agent:**

> Prepare this personal blog for GitHub Pages. Inspect its configuration,
> render it, and explain the files and repository settings needed. Show
> the destination and intended visibility. Stop before creating a remote
> repository, pushing, or publishing.

**Check:** you recognize the account, repository name, visibility, and content.

The next slide uses Quarto's `gh-pages` method for **your new blog**.
This workshop itself serves committed `docs/` from `main`.

::: {.notes}
Publishing workflow: https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/github-pages.html
(checked 2026-10-06). Approval here makes the classroom's proposed destination
concrete before students expose content publicly.
:::

## Publishing Your Blog

After reviewing the destination, **ask your coding agent:**

> Commit the reviewed blog files, create a public GitHub repository
> named my-blog under my account, push the source, and publish using
> Quarto's gh-pages method. Check deployment and give me the live URL.

**Commands involved, after the reviewed local commit:**

```bash
gh auth status
# If needed, complete gh auth login yourself.
gh repo create my-blog --public --source=. --push
quarto publish gh-pages
```

**Check:** open the live URL and test a post link after deployment completes.

::: {.notes}
Replace my-blog with the student's chosen available repository name. Students
complete authentication themselves. The agent should honor branch protection and
use a PR where required. Do not run these commands in the workshop checkout.
GitHub CLI reference: https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_repo_create (checked 2026-10-06).
:::

## When a Build Fails

**Ask your coding agent:** include the failed command, exact error, and file path.

> Running quarto render fails in posts/wine-chemistry/index.qmd with
> the error below. Reproduce it, identify the cause, fix it, and rerun
> the full build. Keep execution enabled and preserve the figure.
> Explain what changed.

**Check:** the same command succeeds and the expected result still appears.

### Exercise

In a disposable copy, misspell a Python variable. Ask your coding agent to repair the
failure, then explain the diff before accepting it.

## Collaborative Blog Exercise

### Exercise — 30 minutes

Work in groups of 3–4. Each person owns a different post on their own branch.

> Create a branch for my contribution. Write a post about my chosen topic
> using the notes I provide. Follow this blog's existing conventions,
> render it, and show me the changes for review.

A partner reviews the evidence and preview. Ask your coding agent to address the feedback.
One integrator combines the reviewed contributions and publishes.

**Done:** each post has a working link, an identifiable author, and a reviewed claim.

::: {.notes}
Use separate checkouts or worktrees for concurrent writers. Avoid concurrent
renders into one output directory. In a protected repository, use pull requests.
An integrator may ask your coding agent to prepare integration, resolve conflicts, and run the
full build, but must review the combined result before publishing.
:::

## Other Inputs, Same Conversation

**A notebook:**

> Adapt my wine-chemistry analysis.ipynb into a blog post. Preserve the computations,
> add the missing explanation, and verify that the rendered results agree.

**An R analysis:**

> Create a post from my R script. Prepare the required packages, add
> captions and units, and record a working render command.

Use the same checks: source, computation, evidence, and rendered result.
